title: Who handed you over?
hook: you'd be furious if someone handed your body to a stranger, so why hand your mind to anyone who insults you? (Enchiridion 28)

segments.voice: Yesterday: a target isn't set up to be missed. Your line was aim at the good. Did you choose one good to aim at, and pick up another arrow after a miss? Day three hundred sixty.

Imagine you're waiting at a bus stop, and the person next to you takes your house keys out of your hand and gives them to a stranger walking past. Take care of these, they say. You'd be on your feet. You'd chase the stranger down the block. Nobody gets to hand over your keys. Now imagine a different afternoon. A stranger in a comment section says something nasty about you. And for the next three hours, that stranger decides what you think about, how you feel, what you say at dinner. You handed them the keys yourself. Today: who handed you over?
screen: `YOUR KEYS, HANDED TO A STRANGER.` → `A NASTY COMMENT.` → `THREE HOURS, GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the comparison. If someone handed your body over to whoever happened to meet you, Epictetus says, you'd be indignant. Second, the turn. But you hand over your own mind to anyone you happen to meet, so that if they abuse you, it's shaken and thrown into confusion. Aren't you ashamed of that? He's blunt, as he often is with his students. The word for mind here is gnome: your judgment, your way of thinking, the place you decide from. Third, how this differs from the insult a week ago. That day was about the moment of sting, and putting a breath between the sting and the reply. This is about ownership. Who is allowed into the control room? A stranger can say anything; that isn't up to you. But whether their words get the keys, whether they get to sit in your mind for the afternoon and steer, Epictetus thinks that part is yours to decide. Fourth, keeping the keys. It doesn't mean never being affected. A cruel word will land; you're not stone. It means noticing when you've stopped thinking your own thoughts and started running someone else's script. The replay in the shower. The imaginary argument on the commute. The urge to check if they've said more. When you catch it, you can ask Epictetus' question, a little amused at yourself: who handed you over? And then, gently, take the keys back. My mind is mine. There's something dignified in that. Not proud. Just a person who knows where their own house is, and doesn't leave the door open for anyone who happens by.
screen: `YOUR BODY, HANDED TO A STRANGER?` · `YOUR MIND, HANDED TO ANYONE.` · `GNOME: WHERE YOU DECIDE FROM.` · `TAKE THE KEYS BACK.` · then, large: `MY MIND IS MINE.`

segments.voice: Notice who is in your mind right now, besides you. Maybe a person from an argument, a voice from the news, a comment you read this morning. Picture them sitting at your desk, inside your head, steering. Don't fight them. Just see them clearly. Then, politely, picture yourself walking them to the door, thanking them, and closing it. Take your seat again. Feel your own breath, your own thoughts, your own quiet. The bell holds the time.
Who handed you over? Epictetus' question for a mind given away: we'd never hand a stranger our body, so why our judgment? Today's word.
Your line: my mind is mine. When you catch yourself replaying someone's words today, ask who handed you over, and take the keys back. Day three hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners notice when another person's words have taken over their thoughts, and deliberately return their attention to their own judgment.

fork.reveal: you'd never let anyone hand your body to a stranger, he says; why hand over your mind to whoever abuses you?

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 28: mind, judgment, way of thinking.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't let people live rent-free in your head.
what it means: you'd never let someone hand over your body; don't hand over your judgment to whoever insults you.
what a scholar hears: gnome, judgment or mind, from the same root as gignoskein, to know; Epictetus pairs it with soma, body, as what's yours versus what isn't.

notes: Enchiridion 28 paraphrased (if a person gave your body to any stranger, you would be vexed; you give your own mind to anyone who reviles you, so that it is disturbed and troubled; are you not ashamed?). Confirm.
Greek γνώμη and σῶμα in Enchiridion 28: confirm; γνώμη related to γιγνώσκω: standard.
Explicitly distinguished from day 352 (The insult): moment of sting vs ownership of the mind.
Bus-stop and comment-section scenes are illustrations.
